title: Greta's Smart Splash
markdown:
The sun hit Greta Holm's window as if it had a municipal schedule to keep. Birds were already at it. She stretched, tasted air that smelled of wet grass, and caught, from downstairs, the far tickle of toast. It was not a gentle Tuesday. It felt like a day that wanted an argument.

She went to the kitchen. Bare feet on cool tiles, a rhythm. Her father flipped pancakes with the practised violence of a man who had been feeding a swimmer for years.

"Morning, Greta. Big plans?"

"Something's cooking." She grinned, took a mug. All week the town had been whispering about a new pool: spectacular, splashy, the future in chlorine. Greta felt the spark and did not trust it yet.

Later she shoved her trusty blue towel into a bag and walked into a square that had become a whirl. Men in sharp suits, briefcases clicking. A giant banner flapped: Pike's Progress: The Future is Wet! In the middle stood Alderman Pike, a big man whose suit seemed to have opinions of its own. His voice filled every leftover space.

"My friends! Today we start the most amazing pool this town has ever seen. Shiny tiles like diamonds. Diving boards that touch the sky. Think — modern!" He swept an arm at a giant blueprint, a drawing in love with itself.

Greta pushed through, boots tapping. She liked water that had a job. She knew a swimming spot from a postcard. She looked at the plans. Big, yes. Fancy, certainly. But where was the deep end? Where were the strong, simple changing rooms a child could use after a proper swim, not a photoshoot? It looked more like a fountain that had sat for an exam and cheated.

Pike, always watching for admiring faces, saw her.

"A smart observer! Young lady, what do you think of this brilliant idea?"

Greta took a breath. The morning sun was warm and unhelpfully honest.

"Alderman Pike. It's big. Very big. But the pool looks too shallow for proper swimming. And those fancy fountains? They'll splash everywhere. Will there be enough room to actually swim, without getting drenched by decorations?" She tapped the drawing. "These changing rooms look pretty. They do not look practical. They look fragile."

Silence, of the civic kind. Pike's smile wavered, then tightened.

"Shallow? Not practical?" The boom lost a watt. "My dear, this is about beauty. About town pride. About showing everyone we are a town that moves forward. A town that welcomes the future!"

But moving forward, as Greta understood it, was not a caption.

"Moving forward means building things that work for people. Not only things that look good for a photograph." She put her finger on a blank stretch of blue. "This spot is good for a deep end. And perhaps some strong benches, not statues that are only for show."

Therefore the square did not cheer. It murmured. Agreement, quiet and slightly ashamed of itself, spread among people who had been ready to clap for diamonds. The grand plan looked suddenly like style in a hurry. Pike pulled at his perfect tie. His face found an alarming red, the colour of a man unused to questions about depth.

"Well. We shall… think about your… comments." The look he gave her was not quite anger. It was confusion, which in an alderman is rarer and more useful.

Greta did not declare the morning amazing. She picked up her towel. Someone, she noticed, had already pencilled a shy mark on the blueprint where her finger had been: a deeper blue, a lane that might actually hold a body. Pike was still talking about pride, but the word had to share the air now with metres and drains and a changing room that would not fold in the steam.

She walked toward the old river hole where the town had always swum, unofficial and unphotographed, and thought of fast kicks in water that did not care about banners. The pool would still be built. Perhaps, if the murmur held, it would be a pool for swimmers. Her bag bumped her hip. The towel, ordinary blue, was ready for work.
characters: Greta Holm (municipal swimmer), Alderman Pike (civic moderniser)
